title: Newspaper web press: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted flex interposer film
idea: Run polyimide film through a roll-to-roll line like a newspaper press: a nickel roller stamp nanoimprints 2 um wiring trenches, slot-die coats seed, and electroplating fills them at metres per minute. The film is then laminated under HBM stacks and the GPU instead of a silicon interposer.
why: Attacks CoWoS/silicon interposer capacity and cost; claims ~5-10x lower interposer cost per mm2 and continuous rather than wafer-batch throughput.

title: Jacquard-loom woven micro-wire substrate with laser-fused crossings
idea: Weave 10 um insulated copper micro-wires (weft = signals) through glass-fiber warp on a Jacquard loom; a punched-card-style program decides which warp/weft crossings get laser-stripped and welded into vias. The result is a multilayer memory-to-compute substrate made with no lithography.
why: Cuts substrate capex and lead time; woven routing gives low-loss round wire (lower pJ/bit than flat traces) and ~10 um pitch without masks.

title: Origami accordion fold: one thinned DRAM strip folded into a stack
idea: Leave 8-16 DRAM dies joined in a strip on the thinned wafer, bridged by polyimide hinge RDL across the saw street. Fold the strip like an accordion into a stack, so the hinges carry the shared bus around the edges and no TSVs or microbumps are needed.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area/bit) and the 20-30% stacking yield loss from bump joins; claims ~2x usable bits per HBM wafer.

title: 3D-printed photonic wire bonds tying HBM base die to GPU
idea: Use two-photon 3D printing (like additive manufacturing at 100 nm voxels) to write freeform polymer waveguides plus printed micro-lenses between silicon-photonic ports on the HBM base die and the accelerator. Because optical loss hardly depends on length, stacks can sit centimetres away.
why: Attacks data-movement energy and shoreline limits: <1 pJ/bit links and 2-3x more stacks per accelerator because placement is not reach-limited.

title: Template-grown compliant copper nanowire forest replaces hybrid bonding
idea: Grow vertical copper nanowires by electroplating through anodic-alumina pores, like crystal whiskers in a mould, on every die bond face. Each 1 um pad touches dozens of springy wires, so stacks bond at low force while tolerating 1-2 um of warp that would break hybrid bonding.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (attacks the 20-30% loss) and removes the need for CMP flatness at sub-10 nm; keeps ~1 um interconnect pitch.

title: Log-raft capillary self-assembly of DRAM dies onto logic wafers
idea: Drop DRAM dies onto water droplets confined by hydrophilic pad islands on a logic wafer; surface tension pulls each die into alignment within 0.5 um in under a second, like logs self-aligning in a river raft. The water then evaporates and a hybrid bond forms.
why: Attacks die-to-wafer bonding throughput (pick-and-place is the HBM bottleneck); claims ~10x faster placement at better alignment.

title: Composite-autoclave batch curing of hundreds of HBM stacks at once
idea: Pre-tack dies into stacks, vacuum-bag whole carriers like aerospace composite layups, and apply isostatic gas pressure and heat in an autoclave so hundreds of stacks bond in one cycle. Uniform pressure replaces serial thermocompression heads.
why: Thermocompression bonding at ~20 s per die limits HBM output; batch isostatic bonding claims ~50x throughput and less die cracking.

title: Gravure-offset printed fan-out redistribution layers on panels
idea: Borrow gravure-offset printing from printed electronics: an engraved cylinder inks silver/copper nanoparticle lines at 5 um width onto a blanket and transfers them to fan-out panels at about 1 m/s. Use it for the coarse layers that route memory base dies to the package.
why: Cuts capital and step count for the coarse RDL that makes up most layers; claims ~10x lower capex per layer.

title: Taffy-pulled wire-in-glass preform sliced into through-glass-via wafers
idea: Stack copper-cored glass capillaries into a preform, draw it down 500x on a fiber tower, re-bundle and redraw (as multicore fiber is made), then slice the rod like salami into 100 um glass discs. Each disc holds millions of 2 um-pitch through-glass vias formed in one draw.
why: Laser drilling plus plating of glass vias is slow and costly; drawing yields interposer cores with ~10^7 vias/cm2 at fiber-tower throughput, for denser and cheaper memory interposers.

title: Co-extruded micro-coax ribbon cables for memory shelves
idea: Co-extrude polymer and copper (like making cable sheathing) into 50 um shielded micro-coax ribbons with 64 lanes each, terminated straight onto memory and compute packages. The low-loss, low-crosstalk path lets 30 cm links run near HBM energy.
why: PCB traces cost 5-10 pJ/bit; micro-coax claims ~1-2 pJ/bit at rack-shelf distances, enabling disaggregated memory without optics.

title: Roof-shingle die stacks with aerosol-jet printed ramp interconnects
idea: Offset each die by 100 um like roof shingles so edge pads stay exposed, then aerosol-jet 3D-print conductive ramps down the staircase to make the vertical bus. No TSVs are drilled into the DRAM.
why: Removes TSV area and stacking yield tax; lets standard commodity dies with edge pads become wide-I/O stacks.

title: Injection-molded liquid-metal vertical channels for reworkable stacks
idea: Mold the stack's encapsulant with micro-channels, then inject gallium-indium alloy like injection molding to form vertical bus lines between barrier-lined pads. A bad die can be removed by heating and vacuuming out the metal, then replaced.
why: Rework turns scrapped 12-high stacks into good ones, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss; self-healing joints under thermal cycling.

title: Ribbon-grown silicon interposer blanks without quartz crucibles
idea: Pull interposer-grade silicon as continuous ribbon through a graphite die (edge-defined film-fed growth) instead of Czochralski boules from Spruce Pine quartz crucibles. Interposers do not need prime crystal quality, and ribbon growth avoids sawing kerf.
why: Cuts reliance on high-purity quartz (>80% one source) and ~40% kerf loss for the large passive silicon used in HBM packaging.

title: Plywood cross-laminated thin-glass interposer fused in one bake
idea: Laser-drill and print orthogonal routing onto 50 um glass sheets, alternating direction like plywood grain, then stack and fuse them at ~600 C into one monolithic interposer. Each sheet is tested before lamination.
why: Mask-free multilayer interposer with glass's low loss and flatness; claims ~3x lower cost than silicon interposers and higher yield from known-good layers.

title: Coin-struck dual damascene: via and trench in one press
idea: Make a nanoimprint stamp with two relief heights, like a coin die, so one press forms both the via and the trench of an interposer wiring level in resist. One etch and fill then replaces two litho and two etch passes.
why: Halves the BEOL step count and mask count for interposer and base-die RDL, cutting capital per interconnect layer.

title: Knitted micro-spring interposer layer absorbing warpage
idea: Knit 10 um copper-alloy wire into a loop fabric; each loop becomes a compliant vertical spring contact between a giant panel interposer and the board. The knit soaks up thermal-expansion mismatch.
why: Warpage limits package size; compliant knit lets >100 cm2 memory-plus-compute panels survive, putting far more DRAM within short reach.

title: Glassblown microlenses for optical vias straight through silicon
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so stacked dies can talk vertically by light through the bulk: reflow polymer into surface-tension microlenses (as glassblowers rely on surface tension) and use reflective silicon plasma-dispersion modulators on each tier to answer a beam sent up from the base die.
why: Eliminates TSVs entirely for data; claims sub-pJ/bit vertical links and no TSV area tax.

title: Sewing-needle stack-then-drill one via through all sixteen dies
idea: Bond the thinned dies first, then deep-etch or laser-drill one via through the whole stack, like a needle through layered cloth, and plate it in one pass. Each die only needs a landing ring, not its own TSV module.
why: Removes per-die TSV processing and compound yield loss; claims ~50% lower HBM stacking cost.

title: Pop-up book kirigami toast rack of edge-mounted DRAM dies
idea: Laser-cut kirigami flex tabs pop up into slots on the interposer so DRAM dies stand on edge around the GPU like toast in a rack, joined by 90-degree edge bonds. Coolant flows between the slices.
why: Fits ~10x more die area within short-reach distance of compute, raising capacity and bandwidth per package footprint.

title: Stalactite bonding: electroless copper grows across the gap
idea: Hold two dies face to face with a 2-5 um gap in an electroless copper bath; metal grows from both pads like stalactite and stalagmite until they fuse. No bonding force is needed.
why: Warp-tolerant, low-temperature stacking that preserves DRAM retention and lifts yield; parallel across whole wafers.

title: Gutenberg movable-type interposer from standard bridge pieces
idea: Keep a catalog of pre-made standard silicon bridge tiles (memory-PHY, power, crossbar), the way a printer keeps metal type, and compose each product's interposer from them in a molded frame. No new interposer masks are needed per product.
why: Cuts the mask, NRE and lead time of custom interposers (weeks instead of months) and frees CoWoS capacity for more HBM attach.

title: Magnetorheological chained-particle z-axis film for alignment-free bonds
idea: Mix nickel-cored silver particles into an adhesive film and cure it under a vertical magnetic field, so particles chain into 1-2 um pitch conductive columns. Any pad lands on several columns, so no precision alignment is needed.
why: Lowers die-to-die bonding cost and boosts yield at near-hybrid-bond density, which helps cheap memory stacking.

title: Sheet-cake cut-anywhere memory sea bonded to logic wafers
idea: Bond whole DRAM wafers made of identical repeating tiles onto logic wafers, then choose product capacity at the dicing saw like cutting sheet cake. Tile-to-tile links are stitched so any rectangle works.
why: Wafer-on-wafer bonding cuts assembly cost; cut-anywhere sizing removes SKU-mismatch inventory and stranded supply.

title: LCD panel fab repurposed to print glass memory interposers
idea: Run 2 um redistribution layers on Gen-8.5 display lines (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, i-line steppers built for TFTs), the way TV panels are made, and dice them into memory interposers. No EUV and no silicon wafer is involved.
why: Huge idle display capacity yields interposer area at ~10x lower cost per mm2, relieving the 2.5D bottleneck that throttles HBM supply.

title: Jacquard-woven passive optical shuffle backplane for memory pooling
idea: Weave 4,096 fibers on a loom into a fixed perfect-shuffle pattern so 64 CPUs reach 64 memory sleds all-to-all with no switches. The topology is set by the weave, like a textile pattern.
why: Pooling recovers the ~20-30% of DRAM stranded in servers, raising usable supply without new wafers; passive optics add no switch energy.

title: Transformer lamination stack with ferrite flux core through dies
idea: Treat thinned dies as transformer laminations: plug a ferrite flux-core post through the stack and wind thick-metal spiral coils on each 65 nm die around it. The core channels magnetic flux so all 16 tiers couple inductively without TSVs.
why: TSV-free wireless stacking made in mature nodes; removes TSV area tax and microbump yield loss.

title: Printing-plate kiss contact capacitive coupling for clip-on memory
idea: Place 20 um pitch electrode arrays made in 40 nm on memory and logic faces, pressed in kiss contact across 1 um of dielectric like an offset plate on a blanket. Data crosses capacitively with no metal joint, so memory clips on and off.
why: Reworkable, upgradeable memory attach with no bonding yield loss, at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, all in non-EUV nodes.

title: Damascus-fold edge wiring: film thickness sets 40 nm pitch
idea: Deposit 100 alternating copper/oxide films 20 nm thick, or fold-laminate metal foil like Damascus steel, then slice the stack on edge and polish it. The face shows parallel wires whose pitch is set by deposition thickness, and this becomes a bridge die between memory and logic.
why: Sub-EUV wire pitch with no lithography at all; claims bridge densities beyond today's silicon bridges for HBM-class links.

title: Decal transfer printing of lasers onto mature-node base die
idea: Use an elastomer stamp, like a water-slide decal, to pick thousands of InP lasers and photodiodes per stroke from their native wafer and print them onto a 28-65 nm HBM base die. The memory stack then gets optical I/O.
why: Optical memory I/O at ~1 pJ/bit with no advanced node; distance-free links decouple memory from compute shoreline.

title: Micro-Velcro hook-and-loop reworkable memory die attach
idea: Plate copper mushroom hooks through i-line resist on one die and loop arrays on the other; pressing them interlocks hundreds of thousands of contacts at room temperature. A stack can be peeled off and swapped.
why: Reworkable stacks raise effective yield and enable field-upgradeable memory; no solder reflow and no EUV.

title: Dovetail jigsaw chiplets that self-lock edge to edge
idea: Deep-etch puzzle-tab edges on memory and logic chiplets so they interlock side by side to sub-micron accuracy, like dovetail joinery, then plate the sidewalls to form edge-to-edge links. The tiles act as a mosaic with no interposer.
why: Removes interposer cost; mm-short lateral wires cut I/O energy, using DRIE and DUV only.

title: Stained-glass mosaic interposer from known-good DUV tiles
idea: Make small reticle-size interposer tiles on DUV lines, test them, and join them like stained glass with printed bridge seams playing the lead came, building panels of more than four reticles.
why: Breaks the reticle limit for memory-rich packages without EUV or risky stitching; known-good tiles lift yield.

title: Vinyl-record hot-embossed polymer optical couplers for memory links
idea: Hot-emboss V-grooves, waveguides and 45-degree mirrors into cyclic-olefin polymer in seconds, as vinyl records and DVDs are replicated from a nickel master. Fiber arrays then align passively to memory photonic dies.
why: Optical coupler cost and alignment time drop ~10x, making optical memory links affordable at volume.

title: Juice-concentrate links: compress in the base die before shipping
idea: Like shipping juice concentrate, a compression engine in the 12-28 nm HBM base die squeezes AI tensors 1.5-2x (exponent dedup, base-delta) before the bus; the GPU decompresses on arrival.
why: Cuts pJ per useful bit and raises effective bandwidth and capacity ~1.5x with no new memory silicon.

title: Brewed colloidal quantum-dot photodiodes coated onto memory logic die
idea: Batch-synthesize lead-sulfide or InAs quantum dots in large reactors like brewing, then spin-coat them onto a mature-node memory logic die as SWIR imagers already do. The die gets optical receivers with no III-V bonding.
why: Low-cost optical receive for memory links in non-EUV CMOS; claims a pathway to sub-pJ/bit memory optics at commodity cost.

title: Factory-seconds HBM: sell partly failed stacks as shorter SKUs
idea: Like outlet garments, stacks with one or two dead dies get fused-off remap in the base die and ship as 8- or 10-high parts instead of being scrapped. Pricing tiers make the seconds a market.
why: Recovers a large share of the 20-30% stacking yield loss as sellable bits, a fast supply gain with no new fab.

title: Tire-retreading remanufacture of DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Harvest DRAM dies from retired server DIMMs, decapsulate them chemically, retest and bin them, then re-stack them into new CXL or inference-tier modules in U.S. remanufacturing plants, like retreading tires.
why: Raises usable supply from installed base; U.S.-located, no wafer capacity needed; low capital intensity.

title: Microbrewery packaging lines: containerized U.S. stacking plants
idea: Deploy modular advanced-packaging lines (panel fan-out, hybrid bonding, laser direct imaging) in shipping-container bays across ~20 U.S. sites, at $50-200M each, the way microbreweries spread. They package imported commodity dies into HBM-class stacks.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability and relieves packaging bottlenecks at ~1% of a DRAM fab's capital.

title: Print-on-demand maskless interposers written straight from CAD
idea: Write each interposer's RDL directly with laser direct imaging plus electrohydrodynamic jet printing, so no masks exist, like print-on-demand books. Small-lot memory configurations become economic.
why: Removes mask cost and lead time, so custom memory-compute packages are cheap at low volume, all without EUV.

title: Cotton-candy electrospun nanofiber dielectric for interposer wiring
idea: Electrospin polyimide nanofiber mats, like spinning cotton candy, to form a mostly-air interlayer dielectric with k around 1.4 around interposer memory traces.
why: Wire capacitance falls ~2x, so CV^2 I/O energy per bit falls ~40% on 2.5D memory links.

title: Self-folding micro-origami antennas for sub-THz wireless memory links
idea: Strain-mismatched metal bilayers on a 130 nm SiGe die curl up into 3D vertical dipoles and horn antennas when released, like self-folding origami. Memory chips then broadcast to compute across the board without package pins.
why: Wireless memory buses cut pin count and package cost and allow one-to-many broadcast; all mature-node.

title: Bookbinding spine bus: plated sidewall links across die stacks
idea: Stack dies like book pages with routing pulled to their edges, grind the spine flat, and plate and laser-pattern conductors down the spine, like glue binding a book. The whole stack's bus lives on its sidewall.
why: No TSVs in the DRAM die, and works for commodity dies; removes TSV area tax with i-line-class patterning.

title: Lost-wax cast microfluidic cooling around taller memory stacks
idea: Print sacrificial polycarbonate lines around and between HBM stacks, mold over them, then burn them out like investment casting so coolant channels remain inside the encapsulant.
why: Heat limits stack height; in-package cooling enables 16-24-high stacks, raising density per footprint.

title: Duplex printing: memory stacks on both faces of compute
idea: Like printing both sides of a page, make DUV nano-TSVs through the thinned logic die so HBM-like stacks bond to both its top and bottom faces.
why: Doubles memory shoreline and bandwidth per compute die without EUV; shorter wires cut pJ/bit.

title: Swiss-roll self-rolling capacitors enabling low-swing memory I/O
idea: Strained nanomembranes roll themselves into Swiss-roll capacitors embedded in the interposer, giving ~10x decoupling density. The quieter power delivery lets memory I/O drop to ~0.2 V swing.
why: I/O energy scales with V^2, so the claimed cut in link pJ/bit is ~3-5x.

title: Standard-gauge memory chiplet footprint like ISO shipping containers
idea: Publish a CHIPS-funded open standard bump map, PHY and stack height for memory chiplets so any domestic DRAM, MRAM or gain-cell die slots onto any base die, the way ISO containers made intermodal shipping work.
why: Creates a second-source market for memory, lowers entry barriers for U.S. makers, and raises supply elasticity.
